1:
The preposition is pressed by two. Ellicott would render it on rather than in, the roll lying on the open palm, and draws an inference from the posture: it was not the will of the Throned One that the book be kept from any. Robertson reads it the same way and calls the language anthropomorphic, drawn from Ezekiel. Gill reports that the Syriac and Arabic have it at or upon the right hand, lying near it, though a later verse makes the book appear to have been in the hand. Wesley calls the right hand the emblem of his all-ruling power and notes that he held it openly, to give it to him that was worthy. Barnes sets the chapter under one design, to honour the Lamb by showing that a power was entrusted to him and to no one else in heaven or earth.

The writing on both sides draws an old reading and two modern refusals. Bede takes the two surfaces for the Old Testament and the New, Scripture’s concordant unity containing the Old without and the New within. Ellicott calls such a division merely fanciful and says the Ezekiel passage that guides the meaning might have shown its erroneousness, since the lamentation and woe written all over that roll indicate the filling up of sorrows, so that the overflowing writing here indicates only completeness of contents. Robertson is blunter: the roll was too full of matter for one side, and the allegorical interpretations of the fact are all beside the point. Clarke supposes a labelled book, bearing outside a superscription indicating its contents.

What the book is has been answered many ways, and Ellicott lists them: the Old Testament, the whole Bible, the title-deed of man’s inheritance, the sentence of judgment on the foes of the faith, the Apocalypse or part of it, the book of God’s purposes. Most of them, he says, narrow the force of the vision; he would call it the book which unfolds the principles of God’s government, the interpretation of life which Christ alone can bestow, and closes by saying that if the aim of all literature is little more than the criticism of life, this book is the key to the true meaning of it. Two of the answers he lists stand in the catena itself: Victorinus says the book signifies the Old Testament, given into the hands of Christ, who received judgment from the Father, and Bede makes it the mysteries of holy Scripture laid open through the Incarnation. Henry takes another, that the designs of providence are fixed and passed into decree, this being a transcript of so much of God’s eternal counsel as men need to know. Wesley cautions against the picturing itself: there is no real book of parchment in heaven, nor does Christ stand there in the shape of a lion or a lamb, but as earth holds something answering such a representation, so heaven holds counsels answerable to these figures.

Seven is read as security by one, as structure by others. Clarke takes it for the number of perfection and infers that the seals could neither be counterfeited nor broken, the matter so enigmatical and the facts so stupendous that human wisdom could not reach them. Henry and Wesley find seven parts rather than one fastening, Henry saying each has its own seal and discovers its events, one scene of providence introducing another; Wesley gives the mechanism, that the ancient book was a long roll on a stick, as we roll silks, and that here were seven volumes wrapped one within another, each sealed, so that on opening the first the second appeared still sealed, and so to the seventh. Robertson reports that a Roman will bore the seals of seven witnesses but answers that this book of doom needs no witnesses beyond God’s own will, and cites Alford for taking the number as completeness.
2:
Why the herald had to be strong is answered plainly. Barnes says the inquiry was to be put to all in heaven and earth and under the earth, so that a voice able to reach those worlds was needed, and quotes the remark that Homer makes his heralds robust men to give them powerful voices; he adds that one of the highest angels, by the mere act of proclaiming it, confesses his own inability and that of all his rank. Robertson says the same in a phrase, that one was needed whose call could reach the limits of the universe. Wesley reasons by elimination: the proclamation was too great for a man and yet not becoming the Lamb himself, so it was made by an angel of uncommon eminence. Gill dismisses the identifications: not the uncreated angel, since Christ is afterwards named as the lion of Judah, nor John the Baptist, and whether he was Gabriel is not material.

The word worthy divides them. Ellicott warns that it must not pass as though it meant merely strong enough: it implies moral fitness, the true strength in the heavenly world, and it was the taint of moral unworthiness rather than any want of capacity that hindered the reading. To commune with God, he says, there is need of no subtle thought, no foreign tongue, no newest philosophy, since the pure in heart shall see him, and Fox and Bunyan can make him known better than masters of sentences and angelic doctors. Robertson keeps both sides, worthy by rank and character as well as by ability, and Barnes the same, since it would take exalted moral qualities to approach the holy God and an ability beyond any creature to penetrate the future. Robertson notes that the clauses stand in inverted order, since the loosing of the seals precedes the opening of the book; Clarke silently corrects it the same way.

The three regions exhaust all creation. Barnes objects that there is no limitation to man in the original, and asks whether angels can penetrate the future any better; under the earth he takes for the abodes of the dead, and wonders whether necromancy is glanced at, so that not even the dead can disclose what is to come. Ellicott corrects the English to no one, since more than mankind is meant; Robertson notes that the prepositions cover the whole universe and adds that the universe declines the challenge. Gill says neither angels nor departed saints know what is to come until it is revealed to them, and Wesley adds an aside of his own, no creature, no, not Mary herself. On the looking, Ellicott offers two accounts: it is usually understood of the look of one who would read, so that none could open and still less read; but it may be that all who tried to take the book could not face the glory in which it lay, as Saul could not see for that light.

The tears are defended. Ellicott says the apostle is not ashamed to call attention to them and that they were no failure of faith but the outburst of an earnest heart; and he quotes the judgment that the words can only be understood by those who have lived through great catastrophes of the Church, and that without tears the Revelation was not written, neither can it without tears be understood. Wesley gives that sentence almost word for word and turns it into a rebuke of those who inquire after anything rather than this book. Barnes reads the weeping as a specimen of two things common to men, the desire to pierce the future, pursued by dreams and omens and auguries, and the grief when such efforts fail. Gill makes the grief representative rather than personal, and notes that the Ethiopic reads, and many wept. Robertson marks the tense: he kept on weeping, perhaps aloud.
5:
Which elder spoke is canvassed and refused. Gill parades the guesses only to sweep them off: not the first of the twenty-four books of the Old Testament, nor Jacob, nor Moses, nor the Baptist, all of these being fancies and conjectures, but a member of the Christian church; and he draws a lesson, that able men may be schooled by meaner ones, as Apollos was by Aquila and Priscilla. Wesley entertains the very guesses Gill discards, proposing somebody risen with Christ and afterwards ascended, a patriarch perhaps, with some naming Jacob, out of whose prophecy the title of Lion comes. Barnes assigns no reason for an elder rather than an angel, yet finds a fitness in it if the elders stand for the church, since heaven had not cooled their concern for her, and they knew what John did not. Robertson sees no ground for preferring any one elder. On the opening words Barnes is brief: tears have no occasion, because the thing wanted can be had.

The Lion is traced to one prophecy. Clarke and Ellicott both send it back to Jacob's blessing, Clarke recalling the beast as the tribe's emblem, reputedly embroidered on its ensigns, Ellicott that Judah's standard in the encampment is said to have borne a lion, badge of strength and courage and sovereignty. Barnes observes the appellation is given to the Messiah nowhere else, locates its aptness in rank, the lion governing the forest as a monarch his realm, and concludes the name fits whoever may break these seals; he too hears the whelp of Genesis 49:9 behind it, the Messiah's descent from that tribe binding title to prophecy and suggesting dominion. Wesley has a conquering prince who can tear his enemies to pieces like a lion. Robertson cautions that Peter gives Satan the same beast, however much the figure belongs to Jesus.

The second title splits the witnesses three ways. Clarke divides it between the natures, root of David as to the divine and a shoot out of Jesse's stem as to the human; Wesley keeps the first half alone, making him as God the root and fountain of that family. Ellicott begins with the royal house, the prophets having described a Branch out of the ancient stock, then presses past it: the Branch is likewise the Root, David's Lord and the ground of every power held by his tribe and by all who look there for strength. Barnes rejects that construction outright. Christ is not root in the sense that David grew from him, but is himself a root-shoot sprung out of David, as a sucker rises from a decayed and fallen tree, Isaiah 11:1; what the phrase establishes is lineage and therefore a right to the throne. Robertson declines to arbitrate and prints both, Root of David or Branch from it.

Everything finally rests on the verb of conquest. Ellicott calls its position emphatic and wants it given more prominence, so that the sentence has been rendered Behold, one conquered, even the Lion; the right to unroll the book hangs then not on divine Sonship merely but on a victory won, and because he conquered he discloses God's hidden purposes to his Church. He ends on an antithesis: in conquering, Christ is seen to be the power of God, and in unveiling the true philosophy of history to be the wisdom of God. Robertson arrives by syntax, the aorist standing first as the great historical fact of the victory. Barnes works from the Greek, which means to come off victor, so that this competence is the fruit of a struggle, and finds a special propriety in leaving the disclosure to him whose conflicts with the powers of evil produced the events awaiting it. Clarke credits the merit of incarnation, passion and death; Wesley has him overcome every obstruction and so earn the honour of publishing the divine counsels.
6:
Where the Lamb stood divides the witnesses. Robertson begins with the seeing itself, stirred by the elder's behold in the verse before, and grants the placing is not quite clear: either close against the throne or in the gap between it and the elders, though he thinks nearness argued by Revelation 14:1. Barnes denies the centre of the seat but makes him conspicuous within the group of throne, living beings and elders. Ellicott is exacter: not upon the throne but in its middle front, so apparently among the living creatures and inside the ring the four and twenty form. Henry overrules all three, seating him with the Father, nearer than elders or ministers. Gill notes that the clause naming throne and beasts is absent from the Syriac.

A Lion was promised and a little Lamb appeared. The word is a diminutive, Ellicott insists, and the surprise carries its doctrine: majesty is rightly read in the Lion, for all authority in heaven and earth is Christ's, but it is authority working through apparent feebleness, the waters of Shiloah outrunning the Euphrates, the little Lamb outmatching that roaring lion who prowls for someone to devour. Henry puts the reversal as two offices, a lion to vanquish Satan and a lamb to satisfy divine justice. Barnes grounds the title in innocence and in the beast most commonly laid on an altar, John 1:29. Robertson counts the diminutive used of the crucified Christ nine and twenty times across twelve chapters of this book, where the remaining New Testament prefers another word.

The marks of slaughter are read as present and permanent. Barnes keeps to appearances: something about the figure indicated killing, John does not say what, and either a covering of blood or the scars of mortal wounds would answer all the picture requires; so the atonement was set before him that he knew why unsealing belonged to this hand. Clarke makes the offering contemporary, as though the blood were pouring now, and turns it to use, that whoever approaches the throne of grace finds a victim waiting there to present. Ellicott fastens on the standing: wound-marks yet no corpse, since it is not the Lamb but the suffering Lamb that is exalted, not the Christ but the Christ crucified who is the power of God. Robertson explains the comparative particle the same way, that he lives while wearing the evidence, notes that the verb for butchering turns up in the New Testament almost nowhere outside this book, and makes him victim and Priest at once. Wesley hears a posture in it: he lies no longer, but waits ready for every office.

Strength and knowledge close the verse, and here the glosses agree while the applications part. Barnes locates a horn's fitness in the brute fact that an animal's might and victories reside there, with seven for completeness; Ellicott reaches the same by the blessing of Joseph, whose horns are those of a wild bull, Deuteronomy 33:17. The eyes mean intelligence able to range over everything, says Barnes, who then refuses to guess how eyes and horns were arranged and calls such conjecture vain; the whole figure is symbol, and no more to be taken for a real many-eyed creature than the glassy sea, the seats and the golden crowns are for furniture. Robertson, hearing Zechariah, calls the eyes omniscience and untangles the ownership: Christ's seven Spirits here, God's Holy Spirit plainly earlier, one Spirit belonging to both. Clarke slides from wisdom to providence, since Spirits of God better suit the world's government and its angelic ministry. Ellicott notices that sent shares a root with apostle, so that an apostolate of the Spirit runs beside the Church's and, on the present reading, is being exerted continually. Wesley ends widest, the Spirit's working reaching through creation natural as well as spiritual, mere matter no likelier to gravitate than to speak.
7:
The change of tense is caught by two. Ellicott notes that the apostle writes came and then has taken, and puts it down to the rapt attention of the seer, whose narrative trembles with his own feeling: he wept a while ago, and now he need not weep, he came, he has taken the roll. Robertson makes the same observation from the grammar, the perfect not standing for an aorist but giving a vivid dramatic picture of the actual scene. Gill dwells on the approach, that he came up even to the seat, which a mere creature without a Mediator cannot do; Wesley finds here the psalm’s Ask of me fulfilled, the taking a signal of the Father’s delivering to him all power in heaven and earth; and Clarke explains it by another, that the only-begotten Son hath declared the God no man hath seen, since with Jesus alone are all the counsels of God.

Barnes alone raises a mechanical difficulty and canvasses two answers. How could a lamb take the book from the hand that held it? One solution makes the resemblance to a lamb hold only of the head, the body being a man’s and furnished with hands; he refuses it, since nothing of the kind is intimated and it is against all probability that the Redeemer be represented as a monster, the fitness of the figure being destroyed if we think of human hands proceeding from the breast. The second is that the form was changed and a human one resumed when the Saviour advanced to take the book, which would relieve the difficulty, the only objection being that no such change is expressly noticed.

Who held the harps is disputed. Barnes gives three reasons for the elders and not the living creatures: the Greek participle agrees with the word for elders, harps and censers are incongruous in creatures shaped as a lion and a calf and an eagle, and the song that follows fits the elders as representatives of the church, since it says they were redeemed by blood. Wesley says flatly the elders, not the living creatures; Ellicott thinks it perhaps more natural. Clarke divides them instead, each of the elders and living creatures having one. Ellicott adds why both orders are present: the living beings represent creation, which groans and waits for the reign of righteousness, the elders the Church, and both adore the Lamb who holds the meaning of life in his hand.

Barnes objects to the English word vial, which with us means a slender bottle with a narrow neck, whereas the article was used for offering incense and must have had a large open mouth: bowl or goblet would be better; Robertson calls them broad shallow saucers, Wesley cups or censers, Ellicott censers holding incense. Wesley calls the harp a chief instrument of thanksgiving in the temple, a fit emblem of the melody of their hearts. That the incense is prayer they all take from the psalm. Clarke adds a rabbinic saying that the odour of Israel’s prayers equals myrrh and frankincense, and on the Sabbath is preferred to all perfumes, and guards the figure sharply: the words are to be understood as This is my body is, the odours representing the prayers. Henry pairs them: prayer and praise should always go together, the harps instruments of the one and the vials full of the other. Wesley narrows the reference, that these are not the prayers of the elders themselves but of the other saints still upon earth. Ellicott quotes the saying that of three sweet ingredients, petition, confession and thanksgiving, the incense of prayer is made, and that when the hearts of saints unite the pillar of sweet smoke goes up the fuller; he ends by gathering every sob from an agonising heart and every sigh of the solitary and struggling Christian into the songs of the triumphant.
9:
The song is called new, and they differ over what it is new against. Gill distinguishes it from the old song of Moses at the Red sea, an unheard of song none could learn but the redeemed. Robertson sets it against the old song of creation sung earlier to God, and groups it with the book’s other new things, the new name, the new Jerusalem, the new heaven and earth; it is new as a fresh song for new mercies. Barnes grants that adoration has always been sung in heaven, but says this one would never have been sung had man not fallen and the Redeemer not died, and that it stays new in being sung afresh as redeemed millions arrive. Clarke thinks new may simply mean most excellent, and hears in the harps the psalm’s instrument of ten strings. Wesley says only that neither they nor any other had sung it before.

The ground of the worthiness is the slaying. Barnes says the death acquired him a right to approach where no other could, and that this is not the only ground but the most conspicuous one. The verb rendered redeemed means to purchase, redemption being by payment of a price; to God means we are henceforth his, rescued from the servitude of Satan. Then he makes by thy blood a test: it is language used by those who believe in the atonement, and not by one who holds Christ a mere martyr or a teacher of morality, since if he was truly an atoning sacrifice the words are full of meaning, and if not, none. Robertson notes that the same verb is used by Paul and Peter of our purchase from sin, and that the blood as price runs all through the Apocalypse, which is why he is worthy to take the book and receive the adoration given the Father. Clarke says the redemption by blood plainly shows his life was a sacrificial offering for the sins of mankind.

Whether the singers are themselves redeemed turns on a disputed pronoun. Gill records that the Alexandrian copy, the Complutensian edition and the Syriac, Arabic and Ethiopic versions read them for us. Wesley reads them and draws a devotional point from it, that they speak of themselves in the third person out of deep self-abasement; but at the previous verse he kept us and inferred that the living creatures also were of the redeemed. He adds that the words look less to the act of redemption, long before, than to its fruit, and so to those who had finished their course. Clarke takes living creatures and elders together as the aggregate of the followers of God, the Church in all nations and perhaps through the whole compass of time.

The four words for mankind and the reign close the song. Barnes grades them: tribe is the smallest, a family with a common ancestor; tongue is larger, since one nation may speak many languages; people denotes a mass made up of smaller bodies, against the other Greek word, used of free citizens on a level; nation is widest, taking in all under one sovereignty. Robertson notes there is no word for men before the preposition, an ellipsis found elsewhere; Wesley compresses the list to out of all mankind. On reigning on the earth Barnes and Wesley part. Barnes reads a prevalence of true religion so great that righteous men hold the offices and the affairs of nations fall to them, and denies expressly that a literal kingdom under the Saviour is affirmed, or that the saints descend from heaven to thrones under a visible king. Wesley reads the new earth, with which the golden crowns of the elders agree, the reign following under the seventh trumpet and after the first resurrection. Robertson adds that the aorist made is prophetic and the present they reign futuristic, some copies reading the future.
11:
A third circle opens outside the first two. Robertson calls it the outer and vaster circle of angels, catching up the new song in antiphonal answer to the living creatures and elders; Barnes says the elders occupied the centre as it appeared to John and this innumerable company surrounded them, showing universal sympathy and harmony in heaven. Ellicott quotes the reason: the highest act of love must be the highest manifestation of the divine character, and so a delight to all creatures, fallen or unfallen; if the Revelation is true, no part of God’s intelligent universe can break sympathy with it. Wesley makes the geometry doctrine: the angels form the third circle, and it is remarkable that men are represented through this whole vision as nearer to God than any angel.

On the number they agree it is not arithmetic, then one of them does the arithmetic. Barnes calls ten thousand times ten thousand a hundred millions, a general term not to be taken literally, thousands of thousands implying the first figure was too small; Robertson calls the order a mild inversion of greater and less; Ellicott says it is needless to observe that the numbers are not literal, and reaches for a poet’s numbers without number. Gill will not put a figure to it, recalling the heavenly host at the incarnation and the twelve legions Christ could have had, and noting the Syriac reading, as the voice of many waters. Wesley alone counts: at least two hundred millions and two millions over, and yet but a part of the holy angels. Cyril computes the other way, bidding his hearer reckon the Roman nation, the barbarian tribes, all who died within a hundred years and all buried within a thousand, all from Adam to this day: great indeed is the multitude, but yet it is little, for the angels are many more, mankind being the single sheep to their ninety and nine.

The second chorus is sevenfold, and whether the seven answer anything is disputed here between two voices. Ellicott observes that the redeemed take no part in it, so its being sevenfold does not interrupt the advance of the doxologies. The article stands before power only, where elsewhere it stands before each word, and he suggests it gives emphasis, since none was able — the same word as power — to open the book, but the Lamb conquered. Then he dismisses a reading: some think the seven terms refer to the seven seals, which seems strained, completeness being the only connection. Wesley holds exactly that reading: the sevenfold applause answers the seven seals, the four former describing all visible and the latter all invisible things, every word bearing a resemblance to the seal which it answers. Robertson takes the single article as grouping the seven grounds into one heptad, against the separate articles of the earlier doxology.

The seven words are glossed twice over, at length and in shorthand. Barnes divides them, some his by nature and some conferred by his work: riches is abundance, he being the original proprietor of all things; wisdom chooses the best ends and means, shown in meeting the fall and in making mercy consistent with justice; strength was manifested in controlling winds and diseases and devils and in triumphing over death; glory is a higher ascription than honour, the one the heart’s feeling and the other its expression. Clarke gives each a single word, omnipotence, beneficence, omniscience, power in prevalent exercise, reputation, praise, and the thankful acknowledgments of creation, matching the seven to a rabbinical form which he says the author keeps in view. Robertson notes the change to the third person, worthy is, where the elders had said worthy art thou; Wesley accounts for it, they being more nearly allied to him than the angels. Gill hears in the loud voice their zeal and affection, that all might hear his worthiness.
13:
The third chorus is the universe. Ellicott says the song of the redeemed, echoed by the angels, is merged in the utterance of all, and that limiting it to the rational or animate creation enfeebles the climax and denudes the passage of its poetry. Robertson calls it a wider antiphonal circle beyond the angels, from the four fields of life, no created thing left out, and hears behind it the agony of creation hoping for freedom from the bondage of corruption: if the trail of the serpent is on all creation, it will ultimately be thrown off. Barnes asks how far to press it. The language need not be taken literally, he says, still less understood of the angels presiding over earth, under-world and sea; it is popular language. He then draws the distinction that matters: in the psalm the universe is called on to praise, here it is described as doing it. Gill spreads it out as angels and the spirits of just men made perfect, sun, moon and stars, and fowls of the air.

Clarke turns the chorus into argument. Creation gives the same praise, in the same terms, to the Lamb just slain as to God on the throne; and if Christ were not properly God this would be idolatry, giving the creature what belongs to the Creator. Robertson makes the observation without the inference, noting only that this doxology sets a separate article before each word and active power where the angels’ song had reserve of strength. Ellicott finds the words appropriately fourfold, and observes that the two preceding songs honoured the Lamb while this addresses the Throned One and the Lamb together, a linking common through the book: here in praise, later in wrath, consolation and triumph. Wesley alone parcels the four words out to the four regions — heaven says blessing, earth honour, under the earth glory, the sea strength — and takes in every creature, good or bad, his enemies acknowledging his glory though only those in heaven bless him.

Then the noise stops. Gill says the living creatures assented, wishing that so it might be and believing that so it was. Barnes notes the symmetry, that they began the work of praise and it was proper that it close with them, the universe left in adoration, waiting for what follows the opening of the volume. Robertson calls the falling down a silent adoration closing the service, and remembers the Roman’s report that the Christians sing a song to Christ as to God. Ellicott makes the silence the point: the Amen rises from universal nature and the Church falls down without words, thought and feeling asserting themselves above language, for there are times when silence is the most eloquent applause. He quotes an old divine, let thy prayers be without words rather than thy words without prayer, and two poets confessing speech too feeble to give conception birth.

Two of them reach one textual verdict by different roads. Clarke reports that four and twenty is wanting in the most eminent manuscripts and versions, and the clause about him that liveth for ever in a long list of manuscripts, versions and old commentators, so that it is undoubtedly spurious and an editor has struck both out. Ellicott agrees that the remaining words are wanting in some of the best manuscripts, and adds a reason Clarke does not: they spoil the graphic force of the description. Clarke then closes the chapter in protest. Now follow, he says, the least intelligible parts of this mysterious book, on which so much has been written and so much in vain; it is natural for man to desire to be wise, and the harder the subject the more it is studied, but of what use has all this learned labour been to mankind? Can hypothesis explain prophecy, he asks, and conjecture find a basis for faith to rest on?
